chapter_theme: Natrinai 41-60 across all five lands: men leaving for wealth and the friend's arguments for and against it (41, 43, 46, 48, 52), homecomings seen by the returning man (42, 59), the girl kept at home and the veri rite misreading her sickness (47, 51, 53, 57, 60), the friend's tricks and rebuffs (45, 50, 55, 58), and the woman alone with her heart, her evening and a heron (54, 56).

41.reading: The friend steadies the wife by the way of the world: men go far and suffer in the waste, easing their weariness only at a small gravel-choked well after an elephant's kick has raised the salt dust, because they want the life in which a young wife, her forehead pricked with sweat from the smoke of ghee-stirred meat, cooks for a guest of good name who arrives at night.
41.nuance: The friend's comfort is not that he will soon return but that his suffering has a purpose she can picture: the household's hospitality. The close-up of sweat on the wife's forehead puts the reward of his journey in her own kitchen, so the absence is reframed as work done for her house.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்டு ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகளைத் தோழி உலகியல் கூறி வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: the man goes far away and suffers on the waste for the household's sake

42.reading: Returning from his task, the man tells his charioteer he cannot forget how, because the croaking of the frogs in the rain-filled hollows would drown the chariot's bells, the servants ran ahead to tell her, and she quickly washed her unwashed hair, pressed a few flowers into it and, without fuss, embraced him in her joy.
42.nuance: Sending the servants ahead is a courtesy to her: she is spared being found unkempt. The poem's whole picture is the few minutes between the warning and the embrace, a domestic haste the hero treasures more than the welcome itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the first rains filling the hollows as the man comes home from his task

43.reading: The friend tells the man that crossing the waste, where in heat that shimmers like spread cloth a starving red dog kills a weary wild cow and its leftovers feed travellers, is a joy to him, but for her, hearing of his going, ruin has come, like the king of a single fort whose overlord, after saying 'fear not', abandoned him when an elephant-led army laid siege and his broken wall found no defender.
43.nuance: The simile turns the hero's earlier promise into the overlord's 'fear not' (அஞ்சல் என்ற இறை): she is the vassal fort he pledged to protect, and his departure is the abandonment. The only food on the road is a predator's leftovers, the measure of what he trades her for.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைவனைச் செலவு அழுங்குவித்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the man's announced journey across the hot waste

comparisons.tenor: the glare of the heat over the hill slope
the woman abandoned by the man who promised her protection

44.reading: Kept from her after her confinement, the man at the meeting place asks his heart whether the daughter of the hill lord, who bathed in the falls with her companions until her large eyes reddened, gave him an unaimed glance and a smile and went home, can know what it longs for, in the land where kuravar wearing kodal garlands rest in their yards after the millet harvest and by the light of fireflies in the jackfruit groves watch the clouds pass.
44.nuance: குறியா நோக்கம், a look not aimed at him, is all he has to go on, and the question to his heart is whether that look meant anything. The closing scene of people at ease in their yards watching clouds by firefly light is the leisure he no longer has.

colophon.thurai: இச்செறிப்பின் பிற்றை ஞான்று தலைமகன் குறியிடத்து வந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill people, the millet harvest and the waterfall

45.reading: The friend turns the suitor away: she is the daughter of fishermen of the shore hamlet who go out into the blue sea to spear fish, and he the dear son of a rich man of the old market town of long flags and swift chariots; we who drive birds off the shark meat we dry smell of fish, so move on, for our small life from the sea is no match for yours, though our people too have their men of worth.
45.nuance: The rebuff is pride dressed as humility: she lists their fish smell and small life only to end on செம்மலும் உடைத்தே, 'we too have our nobles'. The test is whether the rich man's son will persist across the difference of station.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishing people and their dried shark

46.reading: The friend tells the man who has announced his going that pleasure and youth pass day by day like the shadow of a shot arrow, which he cannot claim not to see, yet he will not cherish them: he says he will leave her jewelled breast lonely, crossing the hard waste where the hot wind blows through the bamboo and the kondrai pods swing like drumsticks beating, held by the desire for wealth that does not last.
46.nuance: Her argument uses the moralist's premise, that youth and pleasure are fleeting, to reach the lover's conclusion: what passes must be enjoyed now, and it is the wealth (மன்னாப் பொருள்) that is the impermanent thing. The image of the bards (line 6) is obscure; the drumstick image beside it is clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the man announces that he will leave for wealth

comparisons.tenor: pleasure and youth passing day by day
the kondrai pods swinging in the hot wind

47.reading: With the man listening, the friend asks the girl what harm there would be in telling the lord of the forest land, where a cow elephant whose great tusker a tiger has killed cannot move for grief and suffers like one gravely wounded, holding her calf with ears like green neythal leaves, that the mother, misreading the sign of the molucca beans as possession, kills a kid for the Murugu rite that cannot help her gold-like pallor.
47.nuance: The bereaved elephant shows what the friend fears the girl will become if he does not come to marry her, and the rite shows why no one at home can cure her. Telling him 'this' (இது) is the whole message, and he is standing where he can hear it.

thinai_evidence.note: the tusker and tiger of the forest and the Murugu rite

ullurai.tenor: the girl, left to waste if her lover is lost to her

pairs.situation: the loss of the lover, which is what she faces if he does not come to marry her
the girl, kept in the house and unable to go to him
her pallor, a wound the mother's rite cannot reach

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the elephants of the hero's own forest land in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

48.reading: The friend tells the man who has announced his parting that even today, as on that day, the forest swirls before their eyes: the soft umbrella blossoms of the kongu shining like the stars at dawn in the flower-scented waste, the bangled bowmen with whetted arrows who came fearlessly at them, whom he drove off in the fight, and the forest where he hid them when their own kin came close.
48.nuance: The memory is of the elopement, when he fought robbers and hid her from her pursuing kin. Recalling it now, the friend sets his old courage for her against his present wish to leave her; the reproach is never spoken.

thinai_evidence.note: the remembered journey through the forest with the girl he took from her kin

comparisons.tenor: the forest of that day, as vivid as if it were still before their eyes

49.reading: The friend tells the girl that the bangled women have gone in from the milk-white dune and the shore is empty, the day has ended with driving birds off the curled prawns spread to dry, and their own men, happy with the sharks they speared, have stopped fishing and gone to rest; so what if they went now, feeling safe, to the small good town of the lord of the clear sea, where the punnai flowers of the common ground mingle their scent with the screwpine of the yard?
49.nuance: Every clause of the first half closes something down (the women, the shore, the day, the men), and only then does the friend propose they go to him. The stillness of their own people is the permission for the night meeting.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகளை இரவுக்குறி நயப்பித்தது சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி ஆற்றாமை வியந்தூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the dune, the punnai and the screwpine of the shore

50.reading: The friend tells the bard how his master, decked in earrings, garland and a small green bangle, jostled her as if a stranger in the narrow press of the long street as she went to join the festival dance, warning her that someone might hear and remarking on pallor, how she answered 'you have no shame, fellow' and came away, and how she had failed to guard the girl because she trusted him, unseeing, as a man even his enemies admire, taking his smallness for greatness.
50.nuance: The bard comes as go-between, and the friend answers with an incident that shows the master's true size. The last line is her own confession: the fault was trusting without looking.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's revelry at the town festival, for which the friend turns his bard away

51.reading: The girl asks her friend what they can do: the rain will not stop, with loud thunder that makes the bamboo clefts ring and angers the snakes and shakes the high hills, and with the rain the velan has come like stretched lightning, and the caressing of her loosened hair goes on, all for the lord of the hill where a killer tusker, its feet soaked in crushed wild jasmine and its forehead caked with mud, has broken the innocent young jackfruit tree among vengai trees strewn with flowers.
51.nuance: Her fear has two objects: the storm on the path he must take by night, and the rite that will expose her. பேதை ஆசினி, 'the innocent jackfruit', uses a word for a young girl, which marks the broken tree as her own case.

colophon.thurai: ஆற்றது ஏதம் அஞ்சி வேறுபட்டாள் வெறியாடலுற்ற இடத்து சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill clefts and the storm on the mountain

ullurai.tenor: the hill lord and the girl his secret love has wasted

pairs.situation: the hill lord has broken the innocent girl's health
her beauty fallen away, the change the velan is called to cure

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses the tusker and trees of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

52.reading: The man answers his heart: he will not leave the embrace of his wife, whose hair is crowned with athiral and fresh pathiri blossoms, but the heart, intent on effort, wants a life of living apart and is never content; it is loveless, for even if wealth came equal to the giving of Ori, the generous lord of the Mazhavar fierce in war, wealth made by toil would be a slight thing.
52.nuance: The hero measures the most he could gain by a patron's giving and finds it small against one embrace. வாழி, 'long may you live', said to the loveless heart, is an ironic blessing.

thinai_evidence.note: the heart's wish for a life of living apart for wealth

53.reading: With the man listening, the friend tells the girl she hid it out of fear but wonders whether the mother knew or simply took pity, for the mother said: the sweet new water of the forest's stony stream, which after midnight rain on the sky-high hill slope comes down with dead leaves and budding clusters, is medicine too; if she drinks it cool, looks on it and bathes in it gladly, her shivering will pass; go.
53.nuance: The mother prescribes water from the lover's own hill. The friend's question (does she know, or is she being kind?) is meant for the man: if the mother knows, the secret is over and he must marry; if she pities, time is short. பனி is both the chill of fever and the trembling of love.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight rain on the high hill

54.reading: The woman begs the white heron with black legs, which after feeding in the curving water longs to fly home to its kin, to stay a little with its fish-eating flock and listen: the small dull evening is deeply lonely; if it knows that, it has love too, so let it tell her plight as it is, not with a stranger's heart, to the lord of its shore fenced with kandal, where the young njazhal whose shoots the leaf-skirted girls pluck is caressed by clear waves.
54.nuance: She calls the shore 'your shore' (நும் துறை), giving the bird a claim on the man that she does not yet have. The heron going home at evening is the very thing she lacks, which is why she asks it to wait.

thinai_evidence.note: evening on the shore of kandal and waves

55.reading: The friend tells the hill lord to keep his truthfulness: he came by night down the stony path among the bamboo, careless of danger, and embraced the girl, and when countless bees swarmed on her from his sandal, the mother looked hard and asked 'were you like this before?'; the girl, unable to answer, looked at the friend's face, and the friend, wondering how she would escape, pointed to a burning sandalwood firebrand and said 'that is what did it'.
55.nuance: ஒழிக நின் வாய்மை is sarcasm: his honest love has forced the women into a lie. The friend's quick wit saves them once, which is her warning that the night visits cannot go on.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை மெலிவு ஆற்றுவிக்கும் தோழி தலைவற்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the night visit by the stony hill path

occasion.words: வரைவிடை மெலிவு ஆற்றுவிக்கும் தோழி தலைவற்குச் சொல்லியது

56.reading: The woman asks her friend whether, in this lovely season when the wind carries the scent bees bring from the small kuravam buds, her heart, which went after the man who loosened her bangles, is suffering with him, unwearied by his task, in the hope of coming back together with him, or whether, since he is not kind, it came back, saw her golden colour lost its old beauty, and went away saying 'she is a stranger', joined to her sickness.
56.nuance: Her two guesses are both about the heart's loyalty, not the man's: either it stays faithful to him, or it disowns her now that her beauty is gone. The poem ends on the word தலைமணந்த, as if broken off.

colophon.thurai: வரைவிடை மெலிவு ஆற்றுவிக்கும் தோழிக்குத் தலைவி சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the kuravam of the early hot season while the man is away at his task

57.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hill that it is bewildering how on his slopes, when the herd of big-horned wild cows rests with their calves by the hill vengai, a tufted female monkey that has caught them asleep creeps up with her noisy troop, cupping her hands, squeezes the swollen udder and wrings the sweet milk into the hands of her untaught young; but when the time to pluck the red-stalked millet comes near, the girl's oiled dark hair will lose its beauty.
57.nuance: பதம, the right moment, links the two halves: the monkey takes its moment while the herd sleeps (துஞ்சு பதம்), and the girl's moment is closing as the millet reaches its plucking time (கொய் பதம்). The friend's message is that the stolen meetings end with the harvest.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the wild cows and the millet field of the hill

ullurai.tenor: the secret love taken from the kin's keeping while they are off guard

pairs.situation: the lovers' meetings, taken while the household sleeps
the hero takes by stealth what the kin keep

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the beasts of the hero's own hill in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

58.reading: As the man leaves after the daytime meeting, the friend curses his horse: may it be beaten with a stick like the sparrow painted on the face of the red-striped toy drum hung on the small shoulder of a rich old family's gold-decked son, the horse yoked to the running chariot of the lord of the cold shore, which took him away at the hour when, with the evening lamp lit at the first drum of Veliyan Thithan of Veerai, the white conch sounding and fine dew forming, we turned back drooping and sad.
58.nuance: The curse is comic in scale, a toy drum and a painted bird, which keeps the anger from touching the man himself. The evening is fixed by a chieftain's court ritual, the lamp and drum of Thithan.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகன் போக்கு நோக்கி தோழி மாவின்மேல்வைத்துச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: evening at the cold shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

occasion.words: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்கும் தலைமகன் போக்கு நோக்கி தோழி மாவின்மேல்வைத்துச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: spoken at the hero's horse as he leaves

59.reading: Returning from his task, the man tells his charioteer that her town, she who lives holding him in her heart with the loving resolve she gave him, is in the hard forest land where the hunter who killed a monitor lizard, dug out a striped frog, cut termites from a tall anthill and struck down a hare, comes home with his load and, forgetting his many wares, revels in sweet toddy; and now that the mullai's fine buds have opened in the woods and the rocks are covered, it is painful too.
59.nuance: The hunter's evening is the homecoming the hero is driving toward: work over, the catch home, everything else forgotten in ease. The last line turns: the season of return has come, and its beauty hurts while he is still on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai buds opening in the woodland

iraicchi.act: the hunter comes home with his catch and, forgetting his trade, takes his ease in his own house
iraicchi.sense: the hero, his task done, is going home to the rest and the wife that wait for him

60.reading: With the man listening, the friend tells the ploughman of the buffaloes, whose paddy stacks stand like a mountain, who goes out sleepless at cool dawn after gorging on a heap of rice with thick slices of black-eyed varal fish, that if he goes with his planters to press the seedlings into the flooded field, he should spare the sedge and the water lilies there, for they are what the dark-haired girl of our house threads into her bangles and wears.
60.nuance: The request to spare the field plants is a message about the girl: she is kept at home now and will not be in the fields, and the man who used to meet her there is told so through a ploughman.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாக உழவர்க்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: the ploughman at dawn in the flooded fields

occasion.words: சிறைப்புறமாக உழவர்க்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

links.note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a household is for caring for guests; Natrinai 41's friend says men suffer far off in the waste because they want the household where the wife cooks for a night guest.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule becomes, in the friend's mouth, a reason for the separation itself: if the house exists for the guest, then the husband's absence earning for it is the rule at work, so the Kural's praise of hospitality is shown to carry the cost the wife bears in paalai.

links.note: Kural 1151, in Parimelazhagar's reading the friend's words: if you are not leaving tell me, your quick return tell those who will be alive. Natrinai 43: the friend tells the departing man his going is joy to him and ruin to her.
links.teaches: Both friends answer an announced departure by saying she will not survive it, but the poem adds the grounds the couplet leaves out: the man once said 'fear not', so his leaving is a broken pledge of protection, which explains why the couplet treats talk of a quick return as worthless.

links.note: Kural 1094: when I look she looks down, when I do not she looks and softly smiles. Natrinai 44: after bathing she gave him an unaimed look and a smile and went home, and now, confined, he asks his heart whether she knows.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the averted look and smile as a sign the man can read with confidence; the poem shows the same sign after the girl has been shut in, when there is no second meeting to confirm it, and the reading collapses into doubt, so the Kural's reading of hints depends on continued access to her.

links.note: Naladiyar 16: the fleeting joy of youth, like a sacrificial lamb nibbling the garland leaves at the slaughter ground, is not found among the wise. Natrinai 46: pleasure and youth pass like an arrow's shadow, so the man should not leave her for wealth.
links.teaches: The two start from the same premise, the speed with which youth passes, and draw opposite duties from it: the Naladiyar says renounce its pleasure, the Sangam friend says spend it in love and despise wealth instead, which shows that impermanence was an argument both renouncers and lovers used, and settles nothing by itself.

links.note: Kural 333: wealth does not stay, so when you get it do at once what stays. Natrinai 46 calls the wealth the man leaves for மன்னாப் பொருள், wealth that does not last.
links.teaches: Both call wealth impermanent, but the Kural still tells a man to get it and convert it into lasting good, while the friend uses its impermanence to argue against going after it at all, which shows the couplet's maxim leaving room for the very journey the akam poem condemns.

links.note: Akananuru 242: with the man listening, the friend tells the girl the mother has called the velan, and the man should come and hold her before the goat is killed. Natrinai 47: with the man listening, the friend asks whether she may tell him that the mother's Murugu rite cannot help the girl's pallor.
links.teaches: In the same overheard situation the Akananuru friend names the cure outright while the Natrinai friend only asks whether she may speak and lets a bereaved elephant show the loss to come, so the pair shows how much directness the overheard speech allowed: the remedy stated, or the danger shown and the remedy left for him to supply.

links.note: Kural 508: one who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble without end. Natrinai 50: the friend failed to guard the girl because she trusted the man without seeing, taking his smallness for greatness.
links.teaches: The couplet is a rule for a king choosing men; the friend applies the same failure to herself in the household and names its cause, a public reputation (even his enemies admire him) taken in place of examination, so the pair shows the akam go-between bound by the same duty of testing the Kural lays on the king.

links.note: Akananuru 292: the girl, afraid of the veri rite, blames the hill lord, where a sling stone flung at an elephant scatters vengai blossom and lodges in a jackfruit. Natrinai 51: the girl, facing the veri rite, names the hill lord where a killer tusker broke the young jackfruit among vengai with strewn flowers.
links.teaches: Two poets give the girl facing the velan the same hill emblem, a blow among vengai blossom that strikes a jackfruit, which shows it was a stock figure for the harm the unmarried lover does and supports reading the broken young jackfruit of Natrinai 51 as a hidden comparison rather than scenery.

links.note: Purananuru 152: Ori, met as a hunter in the wilds, gives a strange troupe meat, toddy, gold and gems unasked. Natrinai 52: even wealth equal to the giving of Ori, lord of the Mazhavar, would be slight against his wife's embrace.
links.teaches: The puram poem shows Ori's giving as so lavish it reached strangers in the wilderness, and the akam poem takes exactly that giving as the upper limit of what a man could hope to gain and still sets it below love, so the pair shows a patron's fame serving akam poets as a fixed measure of wealth.

links.note: Kural 616: effort produces prosperity and its lack ushers in poverty. Natrinai 52: the heart set on ஆள்வினை is loveless, and wealth made by toil is a slight thing.
links.teaches: The Kural makes effort the source of fortune and the duty of a man; the husband of Natrinai 52 calls the heart that obeys that duty loveless and declares its fruit slight, so read together they show that the ethics of ஆள்வினை and the akam of the home make incompatible claims on the same man.

links.note: Kural 1102: medicine for a disease is something other than it, but for the sickness this woman gives, she herself is the cure. Natrinai 53: the mother prescribes the stream water from the lover's hill as medicine for the girl's shivering.
links.teaches: The couplet states as a paradox that the cause of love-sickness is its only cure; the poem shows the mother unknowingly obeying it, sending the girl to water that comes from the lover's own hill, and the friend reports it so that the man listening learns he is the medicine and must come to marry.

links.note: Kural 1226: she did not know evening brings sickness while he who wed her had not left. Natrinai 54: the small dull evening is deeply lonely, she tells a heron going home to its kin, and begs it to carry her plight to him.
links.teaches: The couplet says evening hurts only when he is gone; the poem shows why, through the heron that at evening flies home to its flock, so the hour that sends every creature to its kin is the hour that marks her lack, and her plea that the bird delay its homing for her is the couplet's sickness acted out.

links.note: Purananuru 108: in Pari's Parambu the firebrand a hill woman lights is sandalwood, its smoke reaching the vengai. Natrinai 55: the friend explains the bees on the girl by pointing to a burning sandalwood firebrand.
links.teaches: The puram poem records that hill households burned sandal as ordinary firewood, which is what makes the friend's lie in Natrinai 55 credible to the mother: the girl could smell of sandal from the hearth, so the trick depends on a fact of hill life the puram poet praises as the land's wealth.

links.note: Kural 1293: heart, do you follow him as you please because the ruined have no friends? Natrinai 56: has my heart stayed with him to return together, or has it seen my lost beauty and left me as a stranger?
links.teaches: The couplet gives only the bitter answer, that the heart deserts her as fair-weather friends desert the ruined; the poem holds that answer beside a kinder one, that the heart is loyally waiting with him, so the Kural's accusation is shown to be one horn of a doubt the woman cannot settle.

links.note: Akananuru 2: a monkey drunk on fallen jackfruit wine sleeps content; the friend says if beasts find unplanned joy so easily, the hill lord's planned joy should not be hard. Natrinai 57: a monkey steals milk from a sleeping wild cow, and the friend ends on the coming harvest that will shut the girl in.
links.teaches: Both friends press the hill lord to marry with a monkey of his own slopes, but Akananuru 2 draws the moral aloud while Natrinai 57 leaves the monkey's seized moment unexplained beside the girl's closing one, so the pair shows the same urging done once by open comparison and once by hidden comparison.

links.note: Akananuru 34: the returning man bids his charioteer hurry past a stag that feeds and guards its doe. Natrinai 59: the returning man tells his charioteer of the land where a hunter comes home with his catch and revels at ease.
links.teaches: Both returning husbands read their own homecoming in a figure of the road, and the figures differ: the stag shows the care he will give, the hunter the ease he will take, so the pair shows the mullai homecoming imagined both as tending and as rest.

source_issues: 43 line 1 is the same as natrinai 99 line 2 (flagged repeated_line); marked as written, as a shared formula for the shimmering heat.
42 line 2 (அறத்தொடு வருந்திய அல்கு தொழில் கொளீஇய) is obscure: whose labour and what dwelling are meant cannot be fixed; the verse is marked uncertain.
46 line 6: பாணர் அயிர்ப்புக் கொண்டன்ன is obscure (what of the bards the kondrai pods resemble); the comparison is recorded with basis uru and the verse is marked uncertain.
48: who is included in எம் (the friend with the heroine, or the heroine's words in the friend's mouth) is uncertain, as is the reading of lines 8-9 as the elopement; marked uncertain.
50 lines 5-7: who is jostled and what யாணது பசலை means are uncertain; marked uncertain.
51 line 7 (பின்னு விடு முச்சி அளிப்பு ஆனாதே) is uncertain: whose caress, the mother's or the velan's; marked uncertain.
51: the colophon names no speaker; the speaker is taken as the heroine from வேறுபட்டாள் and the poem's address to தோழி.
56 ends on the participle தலைமணந்த, with the inverted order of poetry (நோய் தலைமணந்த qualifying the heart of line 5); no line seems lost.
44, 49, 53, 54, 56, 59, 60: lines repaired by show (tamilvu.org reading, lost -ஒடு vowel sign, ஃ encoding) are marked as repaired.
